source.title: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie
source.attribution: Andrew Carnegie, Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Cheerfulness is a habit you can grow, not just a trait you're born with
cards.body:
Carnegie credited his good humour to a grandfather who, at seventy-five, was still out on New Year's Eve in disguise, frightening his old lady friends. Friends said Carnegie made "all his ducks swans." But he did not treat this as pure luck of birth. He told young people that a sunny outlook can be cultivated, the way you would move your body out of the shade.

That is a useful reframe. Mood is partly temperament, but it is also attention: what you dwell on, what you laugh at, how quickly you let small troubles go. Treat cheerfulness like fitness, something you practise daily rather than something you either have or lack.
cards.quote: A sunny disposition is worth more than fortune. Young people should know that it can be cultivated; that the mind like the body can be moved from the shade into sunshine.
cards.apply_it: The next time something small goes wrong today, name one thing about it you can laugh at, and say it out loud to someone.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie tell young people about a sunny disposition?
options: It is fixed at birth and cannot change
It can be cultivated, like moving from shade into sunshine
It matters less than making a fortune
It only comes with old age
quiz.explanation: He believed the mind, like the body, can be moved from the shade into the sunshine, and that this was worth more than fortune.

cards.title: You can laugh off most troubles, but not the ones you caused yourself
cards.body:
Carnegie believed most trouble could be laughed away, with one exception. If the pain comes from your own wrongdoing, no amount of good humour will wash it out. He pictured an inner judge sitting in a supreme court who can never be fooled.

He took a line from Robert Burns as his life rule: "Thine own reproach alone do fear." He said this motto had meant more to him than all the sermons he ever heard. The practical point is freeing: you cannot control every misfortune, but you can avoid the one kind of trouble that never fades, the kind you would have to reproach yourself for.
cards.quote: The judge within sits in the supreme court and can never be cheated.
cards.apply_it: Before your next tempting shortcut, ask: will I be able to think about this tonight without wincing? Let that answer decide.

quiz.question: Which kind of trouble did Carnegie say could not be laughed away?
quiz.explanation: He thought most trouble could be shed with humour, but the inner judge who sees your own wrongdoing can never be cheated.

cards.title: Your real edge may be choosing people who know more than you
cards.body:
As a small boy Carnegie kept rabbits, and he talked his friends into spending their Saturdays gathering dandelions and clover to feed them. Their only pay was having a baby rabbit named after them. He later admitted it was a hard bargain, but he saw in it the first sign of the skill his whole fortune rested on.

He said his success came less from what he knew himself than from spotting and choosing people who knew better. He never understood steam machinery, he wrote, but he tried hard to understand people. For anyone leading a team or a project, that is the job: know the work well enough to judge who is best at it, then let them do it.
cards.quote: a success not to be attributed to what I have known or done myself, but to the faculty of knowing and choosing others who did know better than myself.
cards.apply_it: Pick one task you are holding on to where someone else clearly knows more. Ask them to lead it this week.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie say his material success really rested on?
options: Knowing and choosing others who knew better than he did
His own deep knowledge of steam machinery
quiz.explanation: He traced it back to his rabbit-feeding scheme: the faculty of knowing and choosing others who knew more than he did.

cards.title: In hard times, the skills you learned long ago can rescue a family
cards.body:
When steam looms ruined the hand-weavers of Dunfermline, Carnegie's mother opened a small shop to keep the family going. In America she did it again. As a girl she had learned to bind shoes in her father's business, and now she took work from a neighbour, earning four dollars a week on top of all the cooking and cleaning. Midnight often found her still at it, while little Tom sat at her knee threading needles and she recited Scottish songs and stories to him.

Her son called her his heroine. Her story is a reminder that resilience is often very practical: an old skill, a willingness to do humble work, and refusing to let hardship take the warmth out of home.
cards.quote: As usual, my mother came to the rescue. There was no keeping her down.
cards.apply_it: List three skills you have from earlier in life that you no longer use. Which one could earn or save money if you ever needed it?

quiz.question: How did Carnegie's mother help support the family in Allegheny?
options: By peddling goods on the wharves
By binding shoes, a skill she learned as a girl
quiz.explanation: She had learned shoe-binding in her father's business and used it to earn four dollars a week alongside all her housework.

cards.title: What children remember most is the parent who was there
cards.body:
Carnegie grew up with no nurse, governess or servant. His mother did everything for her boys, and his father was their guide and friend. Looking back as one of the richest men alive, he wrote that this close daily contact was the most precious advantage a child could have, worth more than anything money could buy.

You don't need to be poor to give a child this. The point is presence: a parent who teaches, talks, tells stories and works alongside the child, rather than handing every part of childhood to someone else or to a screen.
cards.quote: The mother, nurse, cook, governess, teacher, saint, all in one; the father, exemplar, guide, counselor, and friend!
cards.apply_it: This week, do one ordinary job with your child, like cooking, fixing something or a walk to the shop, and talk the whole time.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie see as the most precious advantage of his childhood?
options: Parents who were closely involved in every part of his upbringing
quiz.explanation: He believed a father who was guide and friend, and a mother who was teacher and carer all in one, was a heritage wealth couldn't buy.

cards.title: Money feels best when it helps the people you love
cards.body:
At thirteen Carnegie worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton factory for $1.20 a week. He and his father rose in the dark and worked until after dark. He took no pleasure in the work itself. But it meant he was a breadwinner, no longer just a cost to his struggling parents.

Decades later, with millions to his name, he said none of them made him as happy as that first week's pay. The size of the sum mattered far less than what it meant: he was doing something for his family. Money that serves a purpose you care about carries a satisfaction that bigger numbers alone never match.
cards.quote: I have made millions since, but none of those millions gave me such happiness as my first week's earnings.
cards.apply_it: Think of the first money you ever earned. What made it feel good? Write down one way your money could serve that same purpose now.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie's first week's wages make him so happy?
options: The job itself was a joy
It made him a helper of his family, not a burden
It was more than his father earned
He spent it all on himself
quiz.explanation: He disliked the work, but earning meant he was a breadwinner doing something for his family.

cards.title: Keep going through the hard job; change often comes to those still there
cards.body:
His second job was worse than the first. At Mr. Hay's bobbin factory, the boy ran a steam engine and fired the boiler alone in a cellar. At night he sat up in bed checking imaginary gauges, afraid the boiler might burst. Later he had to dip spools in oil, and the smell made him sick every day.

He hid all this from his parents, who had troubles enough, and kept asking himself what his hero Wallace would do. His answer: never give up. The break came when Hay needed someone to write his bills. Persistence doesn't mean suffering alone forever, but staying in the game long enough for an opening to appear is often what moves you forward.
cards.quote: Of one thing I was sure, he ought never to give up.
cards.apply_it: If you're in a job you dislike, write down one sign of the opening you're waiting for, and one person you could talk to honestly about how hard it is.

quiz.question: What eventually got Carnegie out of the boiler cellar?
options: His employer needed someone who could write bills and figure
He quit and found a new job the next day
His parents complained to Mr. Hay
quiz.explanation: Mr. Hay had no clerk and was a poor penman, so Carnegie's good handwriting and figuring moved him to office work.

cards.title: Learn the skill your next job will need, not just the one you have
cards.body:
At the bobbin factory, the teenage Carnegie kept Mr. Hay's books in single entry. Then he heard that all the great firms used double-entry bookkeeping. Nobody required him to learn it. He talked it over with three friends, and that winter the four of them went to night school in Pittsburgh together to learn the larger system.

Two habits are worth copying. He looked one level above his current work to see what bigger players did, and he learned with friends, which makes it far easier to keep turning up on cold evenings. Accounting later became one of the pillars of his business.
cards.quote: So the four of us went to a Mr. Williams in Pittsburgh and learned double-entry bookkeeping.
cards.apply_it: Name one skill people a level above you use every day. Find a short course or book on it, and invite a friend to learn it with you.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie and his friends go to night school?
options: To learn double-entry bookkeeping, the system great firms used
quiz.explanation: He handled single-entry books but heard that all great firms used double entry, so he and three friends learned it in night school.

cards.title: When the door opens, say you can start right now
cards.body:
At fourteen Carnegie went to interview as a telegraph messenger. He left his father waiting outside and went up alone. He was honest: he didn't know Pittsburgh and might not be strong enough, but all he wanted was a trial. When the manager asked how soon he could come, he said he could stay that very day.

He later urged young people to think about that answer. If he had gone home first, something might have changed, or another boy might have been sent for. When a real opportunity is offered, delay is a risk of its own. Say yes while it is in front of you, then learn the job fast.
cards.quote: It is a great mistake not to seize the opportunity.
cards.apply_it: Think of an offer or opening you've been 'thinking about' for weeks. Take one concrete step on it today.

quiz.question: When asked how soon he could start as a messenger, what did Carnegie say?
options: After talking it over with his family
When he had learned the city
quiz.explanation: He said he could start at once, reasoning that if he waited, another boy might be sent for.

cards.title: Never underestimate the person who started by sweeping the floor
cards.body:
Carnegie and his friends Davy McCargo and Bob Pitcairn were the three Scottish boys who delivered telegrams for the Eastern line, for two and a half dollars a week. Each morning they took turns sweeping the office. Others who later ran big firms started the same way. All three rose high: McCargo and Pitcairn both became railway superintendents.

Carnegie also noticed that messenger work put a boy in front of the city's leading men every day, and that wise men are always on the lookout for capable youngsters. A humble role can be a front-row seat. Do it well, be noticed for being prompt and reliable, and don't assume the comfortable heir is the one who will get ahead.
cards.quote: It is not the rich man's son that the young struggler for advancement has to fear in the race of life, nor his nephew, nor his cousin.
cards.apply_it: In your most humble current task, pick one way to be noticeably reliable this week, such as early, prompt or thorough.

quiz.question: Who did Carnegie say the young striver should watch out for as a rival?
options: The 'dark horse' who begins by sweeping out the office
quiz.explanation: He said it isn't the rich man's son to fear, but the boy who starts at the bottom by sweeping the office.

cards.title: Settle a recurring squabble by changing the rules, not refereeing each fight
cards.body:
Messenger boys could charge an extra ten cents for telegrams delivered beyond a certain distance. These 'dime messages' became the only real source of quarrels: boys were accused of taking them out of turn. Young Carnegie proposed pooling all the extra dimes and dividing the cash equally at the end of each week. He was made treasurer.

Peace and good humour followed. He called it cooperation and his first try at financial organisation. When the same argument keeps flaring up, the fix is often a fairer system, not a better referee. Remove the thing worth fighting over and the fighting usually stops.
cards.quote: I was appointed treasurer. Peace and good-humor reigned ever afterwards.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recurring fight at home or work over who gets something. Draft a simple pool, rota or rule that removes the reason to argue.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie end the quarrels over 'dime messages'?
options: He reported the boys to the manager
He took all the dime messages himself
The boys pooled the extra money and split it equally each week
quiz.explanation: Pooling the earnings and dividing them weekly removed the reason to fight, and peace reigned afterwards.

cards.title: A borrowed book a week can change the course of a life
cards.body:
Messenger boys worked long hours, and Carnegie's family had no money for books. Then Colonel James Anderson opened his private library of four hundred volumes to working boys. Each Saturday they could borrow a book and swap it the next week, and the Colonel acted as librarian himself. When clerks and messengers were at first left out, young Carnegie wrote to a newspaper arguing they were working boys too, and the Colonel widened the rule.

Carnegie carried a book everywhere and read in every spare moment: Macaulay, Bancroft's history, Lamb's essays. He said he would not trade the love of reading this gave him for all the millions ever made. A steady habit of reading, even in stolen minutes, compounds over a lifetime.
cards.quote: the windows were opened in the walls of my dungeon through which the light of knowledge streamed in.
cards.locator: Chapter IV. Colonel Anderson and Books ¶4
cards.apply_it: Get a library card if you don't have one. Borrow one book this week and carry it with you for the gaps in your day.

quiz.question: What did Colonel Anderson do for the working boys of Pittsburgh?
options: Opened his library to them each Saturday and served as librarian
Paid for them to go to university
Gave each boy a set of books to keep
quiz.explanation: He lent books from his 400-volume library every Saturday, acting as librarian himself.

cards.title: Let children see the family budget and they'll understand the choices
cards.body:
As a teenager, Carnegie knew every week exactly what his father, his mother and he himself had earned, and where every dollar went. The family talked together about each small addition to their furniture and clothing, and every new thing bought was a shared joy.

The other messenger boys called him mean because he didn't spend his extra dimes. They didn't know every penny was needed at home. Being included gave him a reason to save that no lecture could. Sharing the family finances in an age-appropriate way helps children understand choices and feel part of the team.
cards.quote: My parents were wise and nothing was withheld from me.
cards.apply_it: At your next family meal, share one real money decision you're weighing and ask your children what they think.

quiz.question: Why didn't young Carnegie spend his extra dimes like the other boys?
options: He was saving for a horse
He knew the family's earnings and costs and that every penny was needed
quiz.explanation: His parents shared every week's income and spending with him, so he understood why saving mattered.

cards.title: Tell your children you're proud of them; they may carry it for decades
cards.body:
While on a telegraph posting away from home, young Carnegie went down to meet his father's riverboat. His father was travelling to sell his handwoven tablecloths and, to save money, had chosen a deck passage instead of a cabin. Andrew promised him that before long he and mother would ride in their own carriage.

His father was shy and sparing with praise, as Scots often were, afraid of making his sons vain. But he grasped his son's hand and said, "Andra, I am proud of you." He died not long after. Those few words stayed with Carnegie for years. If you feel pride in someone, don't assume they know it. Say it.
cards.quote: Those words rang in my ear and warmed my heart for years and years.
cards.apply_it: Tell one of your children, or someone you mentor, one specific thing you're proud of them for, today.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie's father usually handle praise?
options: He was very saving of praise, so his rare words meant a great deal
He never spoke to his sons
quiz.explanation: He was reserved and sparing with praise, which is why 'Andra, I am proud of you' stayed with his son for years.

cards.title: Remember your own near-misses before you judge someone else's
cards.body:
As a young railway clerk, Carnegie was sent to collect the monthly pay-rolls and cheques. Riding home on the locomotive, he tucked the package under his waistcoat, and the jolting shook it out. A kind engineer reversed the engine, and they found it lying at the edge of a stream, a few feet from the water.

That one slip could have ruined his career. Ever after, he refused to be too hard on a young person who made a bad mistake or two. He remembered how close he had come. A good leader keeps their own lucky escapes in mind and gives others the same second chance they once needed.
cards.quote: I have never since believed in being too hard on a young man, even if he does commit a dreadful mistake or two
cards.apply_it: Recall a mistake early in your career that could have gone badly. Next time someone junior slips, start the conversation from that memory.

quiz.question: What lesson did Carnegie take from nearly losing the pay-roll package?
options: Never carry valuables on a train
Not to be too hard on young people who make a dreadful mistake
To keep all mistakes secret forever
quiz.explanation: Remembering how close he came to ruin made him lenient toward young people's mistakes.

cards.title: Do something beyond your job description, and be prepared before you do
cards.body:
One morning an accident had stalled every train on the division and his boss, Thomas Scott, could not be found. Only the superintendent was allowed to give train orders. Carnegie, still a teenage clerk, gave them anyway in Scott's name, watched every tick of the instrument and took extra precautions until all was running smoothly. He knew he risked dismissal.

Scott said nothing to him, but told others with pride, and soon rarely gave train orders himself. Carnegie's lesson was to do something beyond your duties that catches the attention of those above you. The fine print matters too: he had wired Scott's orders many times and knew exactly what to do. Boldness worked because preparation came first.
cards.quote: the great aim of every boy should be to do something beyond the sphere of his duties--something which attracts the attention of those over him.
cards.apply_it: Identify one problem just outside your role that you understand well. Offer to solve it, explaining exactly how you'd do it safely.

quiz.question: Why could Carnegie safely run the trains in Scott's name?
options: He had often wired Scott's orders and knew exactly what to do
He had been formally trained as a superintendent
quiz.explanation: He had sent Scott's orders many times, so his bold step rested on real preparation.

cards.title: Small kindnesses to people who can't repay you come back in surprising ways
cards.body:
Years earlier, a blacksmith had come to Carnegie's office looking for work. There was none in Pittsburgh, but Carnegie took the trouble to telegraph Altoona, checked the man's references, and gave him a pass. Later, walking home in the dark, Carnegie was quietly approached by that same man, now settled with his family and grateful, who warned him of trouble brewing in the shops.

Carnegie said he met many such cases: a father helped through the lines in wartime to reach a wounded son, a trifling favour long forgotten. He found these returns the sweetest, because a kindness to a poor working man is disinterested. You do it for its own sake, and it comes back anyway.
cards.quote: Slight attentions or a kind word to the humble often bring back reward as great as it is unlooked for. No kind action is ever lost.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Superintendent of the Pennsylvania ¶7
cards.apply_it: Do one small favour today for someone who can do nothing for you: an introduction, a reference, or ten minutes of real help.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie think kindness to the humble was especially rewarding?
options: It made him look good in the newspapers
It was required by the railroad
It was disinterested, done with no thought of repayment
quiz.explanation: He said such acts are disinterested, so the reward is sweeter than doing a favour for someone who could repay it.

cards.title: Your first income from savings shows you what money can do
cards.body:
Thomas Scott offered to buy young Carnegie ten shares of Adams Express for $500. He didn't have fifty dollars, but he didn't want to miss the chance. His mother took a steamer to her brother, mortgaged the family's partly paid house, and came back with the money.

Soon a white envelope arrived addressed to "Andrew Carnegie, Esquire", holding a ten-dollar dividend cheque. It was the first money he had not worked for with the sweat of his brow. He showed it to his friends under the trees, and they resolved to save and invest together. Seeing money earn money changes how you think about saving.
cards.quote: It gave me the first penny of revenue from capital--something that I had not worked for with the sweat of my brow.
cards.apply_it: Look at your savings: does any of it earn something for you? Read up on one simple, low-cost way to put a small sum to work.

quiz.question: What made Carnegie cry "Eureka!" over a ten-dollar cheque?
options: It was his first income from capital rather than his own labour
It was a prize for an essay
quiz.explanation: The Adams Express dividend was the first money earned by his capital, not by his work.

cards.title: When you spot a good idea, act on it before it cools
cards.body:
On a train in Ohio, a farmer-looking man with a small green bag showed Carnegie a model of a car for night travel. It was T.T. Woodruff, inventor of the sleeping car. Carnegie saw at once how important it was. He couldn't get the idea out of his head, hurried back to press it on his boss, and had the inventor sent for.

Woodruff offered him an eighth share. Carnegie had no money, so he asked the local banker for a loan of $217.50, which the banker gladly gave. The cars' earnings paid the instalments, and it was the first considerable sum he made. Recognising an idea is common; following through quickly is rare.
cards.quote: Its importance flashed upon me.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Superintendent of the Pennsylvania ¶10
cards.apply_it: Write down the best idea you've had this month. Take one step on it within 48 hours: a call, a sketch, a conversation with someone who can help.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie pay for his first share in the sleeping-car venture?
options: With a bank loan, repaid from the cars' earnings
quiz.explanation: He borrowed $217.50 from a local banker, and the cars' monthly receipts covered the instalments.

cards.title: As parents age, love can mean persuading them to accept help
cards.body:
For years Carnegie's mother had cooked, cleaned, washed and mended for her two boys. When the family moved to Altoona, it was decided they needed a servant, and she resisted fiercely. Those tasks were her life and her way of loving them.

Carnegie put his arms around her and pleaded. She had done everything for her sons; now it was their turn. Let us be partners, he said, and think what is best for each other. She finally agreed and began going out, visiting neighbours and enjoying herself. Helping an ageing parent often means honouring what their work has meant, then gently inviting them to rest.
cards.quote: let us be partners and let us always think what is best for each other.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Superintendent of the Pennsylvania ¶17
cards.apply_it: Is there a task an older relative insists on doing alone? Offer help this week by first thanking them for all they've done.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie win his mother over to accepting help at home?
options: By arguing she was too old
By hugging her and proposing they be partners who think of each other
quiz.explanation: He put his arms around her, thanked her, and asked that they be partners thinking what was best for each other.

cards.title: Treasure the friend who tells you what to improve
cards.body:
In his twenties Carnegie became friends with the Addison family, highly educated people whose daughters spoke several languages. Through them he first saw how wide the gap was between himself and the well educated. Leila Addison undertook to polish the 'rough diamond', as he put it.

He began to watch his language, read the English classics eagerly, speak more gently and dress less roughly. He called her his best friend precisely because she was his severest critic. Friends who only flatter feel good; friends who help you grow are rarer and worth more. When someone cares enough to tell you the truth kindly, take it as a gift.
cards.quote: She was my best friend, because my severest critic.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Superintendent of the Pennsylvania ¶45
cards.apply_it: Ask one trusted friend: what's one thing I could do better? Listen without defending yourself, and thank them.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie call Leila Addison his best friend?
options: She introduced him to Mr. Scott
She was his severest critic and helped him improve
quiz.explanation: Her honest criticism pushed him to improve his speech, reading, manners and dress.

cards.title: Don't set your team's pace by your own stamina
cards.body:
Made a division superintendent at twenty-four, Carnegie faced a brutal winter on a poorly built line. Cast-iron rail fittings broke by the dozen in a single night, and wrecks were constant. Once he was on the line day and night for eight days, snatching half-hour naps in a dirty freight car.

He never felt fatigue himself, and he later admitted that this made him perhaps the most inconsiderate superintendent ever. He overworked his men and ignored the limits of human endurance. It is an honest warning for driven people: your energy is not the standard. Leaders who can run on little sleep need to deliberately check on those who cannot.
cards.quote: I overworked the men and was not careful enough in considering the limits of human endurance.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Superintendent of the Pennsylvania ¶31
cards.apply_it: Ask each person on your team how their workload feels on a scale of 1 to 10. Act on any answer above 7.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie admit about his time as a young superintendent?
options: He overworked his men because he never felt tired himself
He was too lenient with lazy workers
quiz.explanation: Never feeling fatigue himself, he failed to consider the limits of his men's endurance.

cards.title: A true friend tells you the hard thing early
cards.body:
Carnegie recounts a story about General Grant. During the war in the West, Grant began drinking too freely. His chief of staff, Rawlins, boldly told him so. Grant was surprised; he hadn't noticed. Then he asked, "Why did you not tell me before?" and resolved never to drink again. Carnegie later dined with Grant many times and saw him turn down his wine glasses.

Telling a friend something uncomfortable takes courage, and it risks the friendship. But silence can cost them far more. Grant's question is a good one to remember: the people who care about us often wish we had spoken sooner.
cards.quote: That this was the act of a true friend Grant fully recognized.
cards.apply_it: Is there something a friend needs to hear that you've been avoiding? Plan how to say it kindly and privately this week.

quiz.question: How did Grant respond when Rawlins told him about his drinking?
options: He asked why Rawlins hadn't told him before and stopped drinking
quiz.explanation: Grant saw it as the act of a true friend, asked why he hadn't been told sooner, and kept his resolve.

cards.title: Build your reputation on quality first; cost comes a long way after
cards.body:
Many early iron bridges in America collapsed, causing terrible accidents. Carnegie's Keystone Bridge Works used only the best material, and enough of it. They were their own severest inspectors and refused to build any bridge they thought too weak or badly designed. Nothing ever happened to a Keystone bridge, and he insisted luck had nothing to do with it.

He said it was uphill work for a few years until your work is proven, then smooth sailing. He thought inspectors should be welcomed, and clean, well-kept workshops mattered more than most people supposed. When one firm's president boasted that his men had chased the inspector away, Carnegie privately predicted it would fail in hard times. It did.
cards.quote: The surest foundation of a manufacturing concern is quality. After that, and a long way after, comes cost.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you produce at work. Invite the toughest reviewer you know to inspect it before it goes out.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie view inspectors at manufacturing works?
options: They should be welcomed, because high standards educate everyone
They were only needed for bridges
quiz.explanation: He believed manufacturers should welcome inspectors; a firm that chased them away was bound to fail when hard times came.

cards.title: If you want the contract, be in the room when it's decided
cards.body:
Bidding for a big railway bridge across the Mississippi at Dubuque, Carnegie found his firm was not the lowest bidder. The board had decided for a Chicago rival. He stayed on and talked with the directors, explaining why wrought iron would bend where the rival's cast iron would snap if a steamer struck it.

By luck, one director had just smashed a cast-iron lamp-post with his buggy, and backed him up. Carnegie won the contract by matching the lower price. His moral: be on the spot when a deal is made, because something unexpected may tip it your way. And stay until you have the signed contract in your pocket.
cards.quote: If you want a contract, be on the spot when it is let.
cards.apply_it: For your next important decision that depends on others, find a way to be there in person, or at least on the call, when it's made.

quiz.question: What helped Carnegie win the Dubuque bridge contract despite a lower rival bid?
options: A lower price than anyone else
Being there in person, with a director's broken cast-iron lamp-post as proof
quiz.explanation: He stayed to talk to the directors, and one of them had just broken a cast-iron lamp-post, which backed up his argument.

cards.title: Know what each step really costs, or you're working in the dark
cards.body:
When Carnegie entered the iron business, he was shocked to find that manufacturers didn't know the cost of each process. They only learned at year's end whether they had made a profit, and some were surprised either way. He felt like a mole burrowing in the dark.

He brought in weighing scales and clerks so the firm knew the cost of every process and what each worker saved or wasted. Managers resisted, and it took years. But it paid off: when the steel mill opened, they knew the first month's profit to the dollar. Whether in a business or a household budget, you can't improve what you don't measure.
cards.quote: I felt as if we were moles burrowing in the dark, and this to me was intolerable.
cards.apply_it: For one week, track every expense (or every hour) by category. At the end, find the single biggest surprise.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie find most iron manufacturers didn't know?
options: The cost of each process until the year's books were balanced
quiz.explanation: It was a 'lump business': nobody knew process costs until stock was taken at year's end.

cards.title: Promote the people who quietly go beyond what's asked
cards.body:
William Borntraeger came from Germany speaking no English and started as a shipping clerk at six dollars a week. One day he surprised his employers with a detailed statement of results in an original form, prepared at night, unasked. Before long he was superintendent of the works, then a partner. He died a millionaire, and Carnegie said he deserved every cent.

Other clerks rose the same way. Carnegie believed no business policy could match promoting those who give exceptional service. Notice who does more than the job requires, and reward them visibly. It tells everyone what you value.
cards.quote: There is no way of making a business successful that can vie with the policy of promoting those who render exceptional service.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. Partners, Books, and Travel ¶17
cards.apply_it: Name one person whose extra effort has gone unrecognised. This week, tell them specifically what you noticed, and tell their manager too.

quiz.question: How did William Borntraeger first stand out?
options: He prepared a detailed statement at night without being asked
He brought in a large customer
quiz.explanation: His unasked, original statement of results, done in his own time, marked him out for promotion.

cards.title: Go by the spirit of a deal, not just its letter
cards.body:
In the panic of 1873, the Morgan bankers asked if Carnegie would sell his quarter-share of the profits from an idea he had given them. Needing cash, he said yes: his last statement showed fifty thousand dollars to his credit, so he would take sixty. The next day Pierpont Morgan handed him seventy. The account had actually reached sixty, so Carnegie had been about to sell for less than it was worth. Carnegie tried to hand back the extra ten thousand as thanks; they refused.

From then on he resolved the Morgans would never lose through him. He believed great businesses are built only on strict integrity, that a name for sharp dealing is fatal, and that you should always give the other party the benefit of the doubt.
cards.quote: Not the letter of the law, but the spirit, must be the rule.
cards.apply_it: In a current deal or agreement, find one place where you could follow the spirit rather than the letter, and do it.

quiz.question: Why did Morgan pay Carnegie ten thousand dollars more than he asked?
options: Because the account had grown and it was fair, not merely legal
quiz.explanation: The statement showed more to Carnegie's credit than he knew, and Morgan paid what was fair rather than what was asked.

cards.title: Working for yourself trades security for a much wider field
cards.body:
In 1865 the railway's president offered Carnegie a promotion. He turned it down and resigned. He had decided to make a fortune and saw no honest way to do it on any salary the company could pay. The men of his division gave him a gold watch, and he never worked for a salary again.

He argued that anyone at the beck and call of others works in a narrow field. Even a corporate president is hemmed in by boards and shareholders unless he controls the stock. Not everyone needs to go independent, but it's worth asking how much control you want over your own work, and what you'd trade for it.
cards.quote: A man must necessarily occupy a narrow field who is at the beck and call of others.
cards.apply_it: Write down one decision at work you'd make differently if it were fully yours. Is there a way to own more of that kind of decision?

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie decline promotion and leave the railway in 1865?
options: He was determined to make a fortune and saw no honest way to do it on a salary
quiz.explanation: He told the president he would not make a fortune by indirection, and no salary could do it honestly.

cards.title: Decide how much is enough before money decides for you
cards.body:
At thirty-three, in a New York hotel, Carnegie wrote himself a private memo. With an income of fifty thousand dollars a year, he would stop trying to earn more, give the surplus to good causes, study at Oxford, and leave business at thirty-five. He warned himself that whatever he took up, he pushed to excess, and that the worship of money could degrade him beyond recovery.

He did not retire at thirty-five, and kept building for decades. But the memo shows a man wrestling early with the question of enough, and he did eventually give nearly all of it away. Naming your own 'enough' in writing gives you something to measure your choices against.
cards.quote: the amassing of wealth is one of the worst species of idolatry--no idol more debasing than the worship of money.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. New York as Headquarters ¶31
cards.apply_it: Write a short note to yourself: what income or savings would be 'enough' for you, and what would you do with anything beyond it?

quiz.question: What did Carnegie's 1868 memo plan to do with income beyond $50,000 a year?
options: Spend the surplus each year on benevolent purposes
quiz.explanation: He wrote that beyond $50,000 he would make no effort to increase his fortune and would spend the surplus on good causes.

cards.title: Watching prices all day clouds the judgment you need for real work
cards.body:
In New York, Carnegie was surrounded by Wall Street temptations: offers to manage other people's money, invitations to quietly buy control of companies. He declined them all. He noticed that when he opened his paper, his eye went first to the stock prices. So he sold every share not tied to his own business and resolved not to own stock traded on an exchange.

He believed sound judgment needs a calm mind, and a mind swinging with the market is half drunk: molehills look like mountains. He also kept a simple rule: never buy what you haven't paid for, never sell what you don't own. Fewer price checks, clearer thinking.
cards.quote: Speculation is a parasite feeding upon values, creating none.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. New York as Headquarters ¶13
cards.apply_it: Turn off price alerts or remove the market app from your home screen for a month. Notice how your focus changes.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie stop owning stocks traded on an exchange?
options: He found himself checking the quotations first and felt it disturbed his judgment
He lost a fortune in a crash
quiz.explanation: He noticed the pull of daily quotations and believed a manufacturer's mind must be calm to judge well.

cards.title: Sometimes the smartest move against a rival is to join them
cards.body:
Carnegie and George Pullman were both bidding to run sleeping cars on the new Union Pacific line, undercutting each other. One evening they happened to climb the stairs of a New York hotel together. Carnegie greeted him: weren't they making a nice couple of fools of themselves?

He explained that their rival offers were destroying the very advantages both wanted. His proposal: unite, make a joint bid and form one company. Asked what to call it, he said the Pullman Palace Car Company, letting the rival's name go first. They won the contract jointly. When competition is eating everyone's margin, a generous partnership can beat a bitter win.
cards.quote: We were destroying by our rival propositions the very advantages we desired to obtain.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. New York as Headquarters ¶40
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you compete with for the same clients, roles or resources. What could you offer each other if you cooperated instead?

quiz.question: What name did Carnegie propose for the joint company with his rival?
quiz.explanation: Naming it after Pullman made the offer easy to accept, and they won the contract together.

cards.title: Most of the troubles you dread will never happen
cards.body:
Pullman once told Carnegie a story that comforted him. An old man who had suffered every ill imaginable, and many more besides, was being pitied by his neighbours. He agreed his life had been full of troubles, but added one curious fact: nine tenths of them never happened.

Carnegie took this to heart. He thought it was folly to cross a bridge before you reach it, and that even when trouble does arrive, it is usually not as bad as feared. Worry borrows pain from a future that mostly won't come. That doesn't mean ignoring real risks, but it does mean refusing to suffer them in advance.
cards.quote: most of the troubles of humanity are imaginary and should be laughed out of court.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. New York as Headquarters ¶52
cards.apply_it: Write down three things you're worried about today and seal the note. Open it in a month and count how many actually happened.

quiz.question: What was the 'curious fact' about the old man's many troubles?
options: Nine tenths of them never happened
quiz.explanation: He said nine tenths of the troubles in his long life never actually happened.

cards.title: Before you co-sign for a friend, ask whether you could afford to lose it all
cards.body:
Carnegie's old mentor Thomas Scott pressed him to join in guaranteeing a large loan for a railway venture. Refusing was one of the hardest moments of his life, but his capital was tied up in his firm and his partners' families depended on it. Soon a financial panic struck, and those who had signed were ruined.

He offered two questions to ask before guaranteeing anyone's debt. Do I have spare money to pay the full amount without trouble? And am I willing to lose it for this friend? Only if both answers are yes should you sign, and then you might simply give the money instead. Later, he summed it up: give money freely when you have a surplus, but your name never.
cards.quote: Am I willing to lose this sum for the friend for whom I endorse?
cards.apply_it: If someone asks you to guarantee a loan, answer Carnegie's two questions honestly in writing before you reply.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie suggest if you can afford the full sum you're asked to guarantee?
options: Consider simply paying the sum outright instead of endorsing
Ask a lawyer to sign for you
quiz.explanation: He thought it might be better to pay the whole sum then and there rather than put your name on someone's debt.

cards.title: Put your good eggs in one basket, then watch that basket closely
cards.body:
Carnegie pulled out of railways and other side ventures to concentrate entirely on iron and steel. He deliberately went against the old saying about eggs and baskets: put all your good eggs in one basket, he said, and then watch that basket.

He had rarely met anyone who became outstanding while involved in many concerns. Most business losses, he noticed, came in ventures the investor didn't control. He also thought most owners missed the gold mine in their own works, the old machinery that ought to be replaced. For personal savings, spreading risk is still sensible. But for your time, effort and career, his rule holds: pick your field, master it, and keep a close eye on it.
cards.quote: The men who have succeeded are men who have chosen one line and stuck to it.
cards.apply_it: List the projects competing for your attention. Choose the one that deserves to be your 'basket', and drop or pause one of the others.

quiz.question: Where did Carnegie say most business losses come from?
options: From enterprises the investor is not master of
quiz.explanation: He observed that serious losses rarely came in a person's own business but in ventures they didn't control.

cards.title: Replace guesswork with knowledge, even when rivals call it extravagant
cards.body:
In the 1870s, blast-furnace managers ran on instinct, like quack doctors trying whatever remedy came to mind. Carnegie's firm replaced theirs with a young clerk who had proved himself, and hired a German chemist, Dr. Fricke, to guide him. The results turned everything upside down: ores with a fine reputation held far less iron, while despised ores proved excellent.

They bought the scorned ores cheaply and won. Competitors said they couldn't afford a chemist. Carnegie's reply came years later: they couldn't afford to be without one. Where decisions rest on habit and reputation, real measurement is often the cheapest advantage available.
cards.quote: Had they known the truth then, they would have known that they could not afford to be without one.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The Age of Steel ¶6
cards.apply_it: Pick one decision you make on gut feel or reputation. Find one piece of hard data that would test it.

quiz.question: What did the chemist reveal about the iron ores?
options: Highly reputed ores were sometimes poor and despised ores sometimes excellent
quiz.explanation: Chemistry showed that reputation was a poor guide: the good was bad and the bad was good.

cards.title: Keep no secrets from your partners
cards.body:
Andrew Kloman was a brilliant mechanic and one of Carnegie's partners. Without telling the others, he was drawn by flattering speculators into another iron company, which quickly ran up some seven hundred thousand dollars of debt. Only bankruptcy could clear him. The news came during the 1873 panic, when the firm was already under strain, and put the whole company at risk.

Carnegie drew a firm rule from it: no secrets from partners. A partnership shares risk, so each partner has a right to know what the others are exposed to. The same holds in any close partnership, business or personal. Hidden commitments become everyone's problem when they go wrong.
cards.quote: There is one imperative rule for men in business--no secrets from partners.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The Age of Steel ¶40
cards.apply_it: Is there any commitment, debt or side deal your partner (in work or life) doesn't know about? Tell them this week.

quiz.question: What did Kloman do that broke Carnegie's 'imperative rule'?
options: He secretly invested in another iron company that ran up huge debts
quiz.explanation: He joined the Escanaba company without telling his partners, endangering the whole firm.

cards.title: Do the work you're best at, even when a grander title tempts you
cards.body:
Kloman was the ablest practical mechanic Carnegie knew, without a peer in the mill. But he wanted to be in the office, where Carnegie thought him worse than useless. Flattered by men who praised his business genius, he left to start a rival firm. Carnegie and his colleagues pleaded with him to stay. It failed, and he died soon after.

Carnegie had seen other able people wear themselves out in roles that didn't suit them, their lives a round of anxiety. Knowing what you do with ease and pleasure, and staying there, can be wiser than chasing a title you're not built for.
cards.quote: How foolish we are not to recognize what we are best fitted for and can perform, not only with ease but with pleasure, as masters of the craft.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. The Age of Steel ¶43
cards.apply_it: Write down the tasks you do with ease and pleasure. Compare that list to the role you're aiming for next. Do they match?

quiz.question: Where did Carnegie think Kloman's true talent lay?
options: In the mill, designing and running machinery
quiz.explanation: He was a peerless mechanic in the mill, but kept wanting the office, where he struggled.

cards.title: Every team needs one captain, not two
cards.body:
When the new steel mill was about to open, an organiser proposed splitting the works between two managers with equal authority over separate departments. Carnegie, who knew neither man, refused. An army with two commanders or a ship with two captains would fare no worse, he said. One must be captain and report alone.

The choice fell on Bill Jones, a former two-dollar-a-day mechanic who became the famous 'Captain' of the Edgar Thomson Works. Carnegie said no decision did more for the company's success. Shared authority sounds fair, but it blurs accountability. Name one person who owns each outcome.
cards.quote: Upon no account could two men be in the same works with equal authority.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. Partners, Books, and Travel ¶19
cards.apply_it: For each shared project you're involved in, write down the one person who owns the outcome. If you can't, fix that.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie reject the plan for two equal managers?
options: Two people with equal authority on the same ground leads to disaster, like two captains on a ship
He wanted to manage the mill himself
quiz.explanation: He compared it to an army with two commanders or a ship with two captains.

cards.title: Lasting love often begins when each person truly needs the other
cards.body:
Carnegie courted Louise Whitfield for years, riding with her in Central Park. She hesitated. He was rich and had everything, and her ideal was to be the real helpmeet of a struggling man to whom she would be indispensable, as her mother had been to her father. Once she even returned his letters.

Then, in 1886, his mother and brother died within days of each other while he lay gravely ill with typhoid. When she visited, she saw he needed her. Both her heart and her head were now willing, and they married the next spring. A strong match isn't only attraction; it's knowing you each have something real to give.
cards.quote: Her ideal was to be the real helpmeet of a young, struggling man to whom she could and would be indispensable, as her mother had been to her father.
cards.locator: Chapter XV. Coaching Trip and Marriage ¶16
cards.apply_it: Ask your partner: where in your life right now would my help matter most? Then follow through on one thing.

quiz.question: Why did Louise Whitfield at first hold back from marrying Carnegie?
options: She felt a rich man who had everything would have little need of her
She was engaged to someone else
quiz.explanation: She wanted to be indispensable to her husband, and his wealth made her feel she could be of little use to him.

cards.title: Keep discovering, and saying out loud, what you admire in your partner
cards.body:
Twenty years into his marriage, Carnegie wrote that when he chose Louise he had only seen the surface of her qualities. Over time he found far more. In every emergency she was the diplomat and peacemaker. She had never quarrelled with anyone, treated people the same regardless of rank or wealth, and was always quietly planning how to help those around her. She welcomed his elderly Scottish aunts and uncles, and charmed them all.

He said he could not imagine life without her. Long marriages are kept alive partly by this kind of noticing: seeing your partner freshly, and telling them what you see.
cards.quote: My life has been made so happy by her that I cannot imagine myself living without her guardianship.
cards.locator: Chapter XV. Coaching Trip and Marriage ¶37
cards.apply_it: Write down three qualities you've discovered in your partner since you first met. Tell them one of them tonight.

quiz.question: What role did Carnegie say his wife played in every emergency?
quiz.explanation: He described her as the diplomat and peace-maker in every emergency of their busy life.

cards.title: Tie everyone's rewards to the same results, good years and bad
cards.body:
Carnegie was proudest of introducing the sliding scale at his steel mills. Wages rose and fell with the price the firm got for its product, with a guaranteed minimum so workers always had a living wage. He believed this made capital and labour partners, sharing good times and hard times together.

He also advised against agreements with a fixed end date, because both sides spend the final months preparing for a fight. Better to run on, with six months' or a year's notice on either side. Whatever you think of his wider labour record, the principle is sound: when everyone gains and loses together, cooperation comes more easily.
cards.quote: It is the solution of the capital and labor problem, because it really makes them partners--alike in prosperity and adversity.
cards.apply_it: Look at how rewards work in your team or household. Is there a way to link everyone's share to the shared result?

quiz.question: What did Carnegie think was wrong with yearly wage agreements that end on a fixed date?
options: Both sides start preparing for a struggle as the end date nears
quiz.explanation: He preferred open-ended scales with notice, since a fixed end date sets both sides preparing for a fight.

cards.title: Ask people what would help; small changes can matter more than a raise
cards.body:
At one meeting Carnegie asked his men what the firm could do for them. A worker named Billy Edwards explained that monthly pay forced most men into debt with local shopkeepers who charged high prices. Paying every two weeks, he said, would be worth as much as a ten per cent raise to careful men. Carnegie agreed on the spot.

That conversation led to a cooperative store run by the men, coal sold to workers at cost, and a savings scheme paying six per cent. Carnegie concluded that disputes are often not chiefly about money: appreciation, kind treatment and a fair deal count for a great deal.
cards.quote: Employers can do so many desirable things for their men at little cost.
cards.apply_it: Ask each person you manage or live with: what one small change would make your week easier? Act on at least one answer.

quiz.question: What did Billy Edwards say would be as good as a ten per cent raise?
options: Being paid every two weeks instead of monthly
quiz.explanation: Fortnightly pay would free careful men from running into debt with costly shopkeepers.

cards.title: If you signed it carelessly, keep it anyway, then read the next one closely
cards.body:
Furnace workers once threatened to walk out unless they got a raise, though their agreement had months to run. Carnegie met the committees. One chairman said: when I sign an agreement, I keep it. Another, Kelly, admitted he had signed without reading it carefully.

Carnegie didn't mock him. He said he too signed papers he hadn't read, but the best course is to carry out what you signed and be more careful next time. He refused to yield to a broken agreement, and Kelly sent the men back to work and became his loyal friend. Your word given, even hastily, is still your word.
cards.quote: I have always found that the best way is to carry out the provisions of the agreement one signs carelessly and resolve to be more careful next time.
cards.apply_it: Before signing anything this month, read it fully. For anything you've already signed without reading, look it up and honour it.

quiz.question: What did Carnegie advise Kelly to do about an agreement he hadn't read carefully?
options: Keep it, and be more careful when signing the next one
Ask a lawyer to break it
quiz.explanation: He told Kelly to carry out the agreement and resolve to read the next one properly.

cards.title: What happens in your name stays with you, even when you are far away
cards.body:
In July 1892, while Carnegie was in Scotland, a dispute at his Homestead steel works turned violent and workmen were killed. His partners handled it. In his own account, the firm's wage offer was fair, and the fatal error was trying to reopen the works instead of waiting; his rule had been to wait patiently and never bring in new men.

This is his side of the story, and many at the time and since have held him responsible. He admitted his name became a by-word for years. He wrote that no other wound from his business life stayed with him. Leaders own what is done under their name, whether or not they were in the room.
cards.quote: No pangs remain of any wound received in my business career save that of Homestead.
cards.apply_it: Is something being done in your name that you've left entirely to others? Check on it this week.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie describe the lasting effect of Homestead on him?
options: He said it was a minor episode
It was the one business wound that still pained him
He blamed only the workers and moved on
quiz.explanation: He wrote that of all the wounds of his business career, only Homestead still gave him pain.

cards.title: Give help where it's needed, and leave your name off it
cards.body:
Carnegie's friend John Van Dyke tells this story. In Mexico he met McLuckie, once a skilled Homestead worker and the town's burgomaster, who had sided with the strikers in 1892. He had been indicted and blacklisted; his wife had died and he was down to his last copper. Van Dyke wrote to Carnegie, who pencilled a reply in the margin.

McLuckie proudly declined the money and made his own way with a railway job. Only later did Van Dyke tell him whose offer it had been, and McLuckie was stunned. Van Dyke added that Carnegie gave many thousands this way, through others, with no name attached. Quiet help spares the pride of the person receiving it.
cards.quote: Give McLuckie all the money he wants, but don't mention my name.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone struggling right now. Find a way to help them this month without them knowing it came from you.

quiz.question: How did Carnegie respond to hearing about McLuckie's hardship?
options: He sent a public donation with a press notice
He offered him his old job back
He offered all the money he wanted, on condition his name wasn't mentioned
quiz.explanation: He wrote: give McLuckie all the money he wants, but don't mention my name.

cards.title: There comes a point to stop accumulating and start giving well
cards.body:
After writing The Gospel of Wealth, Carnegie felt he had to live by it: stop struggling for more and turn to the harder task of giving wisely. His company was earning forty million dollars a year and could have earned far more. In 1901 he sold it, and declined an extra sum for the common stock, which Morgan said could have been a hundred million dollars more. He had enough.

His first gift went to the men in the mills: four million dollars for accident relief and old-age pensions. He believed giving wisely was more serious and difficult than making the money. Generosity takes as much thought as earning.
cards.quote: I resolved to stop accumulating and begin the infinitely more serious and difficult task of wise distribution.
cards.apply_it: Decide one cause you care about and set a regular amount, however small, to give to it. Spend an hour checking how well it uses money.

quiz.question: Who received Carnegie's first gift after he sold his company?
options: The workmen in his mills, for accident relief and pensions
quiz.explanation: He called it an acknowledgment of the deep debt he owed to the workmen who had helped his success.

cards.title: Ask people to share the cost, and you'll learn what they truly need
cards.body:
Carnegie gave thousands of church organs, starting with one for his father's small congregation. At first he paid the full price, and requests flooded in. Some tiny churches ordered organs big enough to split the rafters, and others had already bought theirs before asking. So he changed the rule: each congregation had to pay half.

He joked that he needed a partner in his sin, but the point was serious. Sharing the cost assured that spending was needed and reasonable. His libraries followed a similar idea: he favoured towns willing to support them as public institutions. Help lasts longer when the people receiving it have a stake in it.
cards.quote: In requiring the congregation to pay one half the cost of better instruments, there is assurance of needed and reasonable expenditure.
cards.locator: Chapter XX. Educational and Pension Funds ¶42
cards.apply_it: Next time you help fund something, a child's request or a community project, ask the other side to contribute a share, however small.

quiz.question: Why did Carnegie start requiring churches to pay half the cost of an organ?
options: He was running out of money
Sharing the cost ensured the expense was needed and reasonable
quiz.explanation: When he paid in full, some ordered oversized organs; paying half ensured reasonable requests.

cards.title: The most satisfying gift may answer a longing from your childhood
cards.body:
Pittencrieff Glen, beside the abbey in Dunfermline, was paradise to the children of the town. But its laird had quarrelled with Carnegie's radical family, and ordered that no Morrison be admitted. As a boy, Carnegie could only peer through gates or over the wall.

In 1902 he bought it and gave it to the town as a public park, with a trust to bring 'sweetness and light' into working people's lives. He set the test plainly: success meant that any child of Dunfermline would feel life had been made happier and better. He called it the most soul-satisfying gift he ever made. Giving that connects to your own story often means the most.
cards.quote: Thus, Pittencrieff Glen is the most soul-satisfying public gift I ever made, or ever can make.
cards.locator: Chapter XXI. The Peace Palace and Pittencrieff ¶35
cards.apply_it: Think of a place or opportunity you longed for as a child. Is there a small way you could open something like it to a young person now?

quiz.question: Why couldn't young Carnegie enter Pittencrieff Glen?
options: It was too far from home
The laird had barred anyone named Morrison
He was afraid of the dark
quiz.explanation: After the town won a court battle led partly by his family, the laird ordered that no Morrison be admitted.

cards.title: When work ends, the friendships you built are what remain
cards.body:
Selling his company in 1901 was a wrench. When Carnegie sailed for Europe, his partners came to the steamer to say good-bye, and he felt the solemn change: this was a farewell. Coming back months later, he felt entirely out of place.

But several of 'the boys' were waiting at the pier to welcome him. They were the same dear friends, though so different now. He wrote that he had lost his partners but not his friends, and that this was much. Retirement or a job change can strip away daily structure. The relationships you've invested in are what carry you through.
cards.quote: I had lost my partners, but not my friends.
cards.apply_it: Message one former colleague you liked but haven't spoken to in a year. Suggest a coffee or a call.

quiz.question: What cheered Carnegie when he returned to New York after retiring?
options: Several of his old partners waiting at the pier to welcome him
quiz.explanation: Seeing 'the boys' at the pier showed him he had lost his partners but not his friends.
